Before the orders of the day are called, I rise to a question of privilege. In the ' Mail and Empire ' of March 15 there is an article under the following heading:

Mr. King declares Berlin Board of Trade did not denounce reciprocity. Record disproves it. Return in Commons shows that he was informed of board's action.
Then appears the following:
Special to the r Mail and Empire.'
Ottawa, March 14.-Another return of resolutions and correspondence respecting the reciprocity agreement was brought down to parliament to-day by Hon. Mr. Fielding. Among the resolutions opposing the agreement was one passed by the Board of Trade of Berlin, on January 13. It will be remembered that during his speech in condemnation of the government's policy Mr. Lloyd Harris (Brantford) mentioned that the Berlin Board of Trade had adopted such a resolution. He was at once contradicted by Hon Mackenzie King.
The file of correspondence brought down today includes the resolution to which Mr. Harris referred. It also includes a telegram from Mr. M. W. A. Lochead, secretary of the Berlin organization, apprising the Minister of Labour of the action of the board and an acknowledgment of its reception sent in reply by Mr. King. The resolution itself reached Ottawa on January 14 and Mr. King wrote to Berlin saying that he had laid it before Sir Wilfrid Laurier and that the premier had promised to give it due consideration.
There is such a semblance of truth in that article that I am afraid the public will not be able to discern the amount of error which it really contains. The statement I made to the House when the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Harris) spoke the other evening was entirely and absolutely correct. I refrained from drawing the attention of the House to this article until my hon. friend, who has been absent for the last few days, was in his seat; and as he is in his seat to-day, I now draw the attention of the House to it. When my hon. friend was speaking, he made reference to an article which appeared in the Toronto ' Globe ' and which led him to believe that the Berlin Board of Trade had, a day or two previous, passed a resolution opposing the agreement which is proposed and which is now before us for consideration. The hon. gentleman, along with others in this country, got his information from a report sent out erroneously by the secretary of the Berlin Board of Trade, and which appeared' in several papers, but in particular in the London ' Free Press ', under the following head:
The Berlin Board of Trade unanimously oppose pact.
Then it goes on :
At a recent meeting of the board this resolution was reaffirmed.
Referring to a resolution passed while the negotiations were under way, and before the present agreement was made known. This article, which appeared in the London ' Free Press ', was copied into Mr. KING.
other newspapers, and also a despatch was sent to the Toronto ' Globe.' It was this despatch which led my hon friend and many others to believe that the Berlin Board of Trade had reaffirmed the resolution they had passed at the beginning of the proceedings; and it was to this alleged reaffirmed resolution, which he supposed to relate to the proposed agreement now under consideration, that my hon. friend referred. My hon. friend is in his seat and acknowledges that in that statement I am quite right. I understood him to refer to the resolution that was supposed to be reaffirmed, but which in fact was never reaffirmed; and it was because I knew he was in error and would not intentionally make an error that I corrected him. The Berlin Board of Trade did in fact pass a resolution when they were afraid that the manufacturers of that town were going to be seriously affected by the reciprocal agreement. That resolution was forwarded to me and I presented it to the right hon. the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister will recall that I spoke of the importance of considering the weight to be attached to an expression of opinion of that kind coming from a manufacturing centre like Berlin.

I have. It is as follows :
That in view of the agitation now being carried on in the United States in favour of a reciprocal trade agreement with Canada, obviously for the purpose of enlarging the markets for the manufacturers in the United States at the expense of Canadian industries and of Canadian workingmen.
Hear, hear.

And in view of the present agitation in the prairie provinces for a reduction in the Canadian tariff.
It is hereby resolved that we, the members of the Berlin Board of Trade are very strongly opposed to any reciprocal tariff arrangement between Canada and the United States which would mean the lowering of the present Canadian customs tariff, as we are convinced that any such reduction would be injurious to Canadian interests. That this board is of the opinion that the Canadian tariff must be so framed and maintained as to continue to encourage the investment of capital in Canadian enterprises and to transfer to the workshops of the Dominion the manufacture of many of the goods which are now imported from other countries, and notably from the United States.
Hear, hear.

That this board is further of the opinion that while our tariff should be primarily framed for the protection of Canadian manufacturers and other Canadian interests, it should nevertheless continue to give a preference to the mother country and also to any

other part of the British Empire with which reciprocal preferential tariffs can be arranged, and recognizing always that under any conditions such preference should continue to afford adequate tariff protection to all Canadian interests.
That was the resolution passed.
What is the date of that?

That resolution was on January 13. I have here an article from one of the Berlin papers which explains what took place on February 24, which was the time at which Mr. Lochead, secretary of the Berlin Board of Trade, sent to the London ' Free Press ' and one or two other papers the statement which led them to believe that the Berlin Board of Trade had reaffirmed the resolution it had passed at an earlier date. I have verified these facts, and they have been given to the public and never questioned, so I will read from this statement:
Unfortunately Secretary Lochead's letter has placed the Berlin Board of Trade in a wholly false light on the question of the tariff agreement, and at the same time has played into the hands of a newspaper that is exploiting the question for political purposes.
In the first place the Berlin Board of Trade did not pass a resolution opposing the tariff agreement. The resolution quoted was passed while negotiations were pending and before any agreement had been reached, and therefore before it was known that the interests' of all Berlin and Waterloo county industries had been carefully protected.
In the second place, the Board of Trade did not reaffirm the resolution passed at the annual meeting in January, as stated by Secretary Lochead in his letter. . . .
According to the minutes there were but six members of the Board of Trade present at the meeting. The motion arose out of a complaint made by several members of the board that proper publicity had not been given to the reciprocity resolutions passed at the annual meeting in January. A motion to reaffirm was, it is true, submitted, but after lengthy debate it was decided that it would be improper for balf a dozen members of the board to undertake to reaffirm on behalf of the whole board a resolution which had been passed at a general meeting at which 150 members were present, and when the members had no information as to the text of the tariff agreement before them. It was also argued that, since by the terms of the agreement, not one Berlin industry could be shown to be prejudicially affected, and that as the purnose of the original resolution was the protection of local interests, to reaffirm the original resolution would be inadvisable. The motion above emoted was then adopted as a comoromise between the contending sections of the Board of Trade council.

Is that an editorial of the
newspaper?
No, it is a news item headed * Board of Trade Council did not reaffirm the reciprocity resolution.'
What newspaper?

The Berlin ' Telegraph,' of February 27 last. So, what I said the other evening in Teply to my hon. friend is absolutely correct, and this item which appears in the Toronto * Mail and Empire,' and which says that my denial proved false is wholly incorrect. I think the facts I have given the House are sufficient to bear me out in my statement.

I accept the explanation given by the Minister of Labour (Mr. King). I made the statement on the floor of the House in perfect good faith, having read in the Toronto ' Globe ' a report to that effect. Since that item appeared, a copy of the Berlin ' Newsdlecord ' has been sent me. That paper gives the date of the passing of the resolution as January 12, and on the 13th the secretary telegraphed to the minister the gist of the resolution asking him to place the contents before the Prime Minister. That was acknowledged. But the end of the paragraph states this:
To make its position stronger, the Board of Trade, since Hon. Mr. Fielding laid the terms of the proposed pact on the table of the House, has ordered copies of the original resolution to be sent to the leading newspapers of Ontario, thus showing that the board considered that it covered the ground'well and was opposed to the pact.
I presume the explanation made by the minister is in connection with this last statement by this newspaper. That was probably at the meeting where the six members were present. However, I am not familiar with the details, and only wish to say that the statement I made on the floor of the House was made in entire good faith.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. CROTHERS AND THE FARMERS' BANK CASE.
PRIVILEGE-MR. CROTHERS AND THE FARMERS' BANK CASE.
speechtext:
I rise to a question of privilege. Referring to remarks .made by myself on the 15th of this month when the affairs of the Farmers' 'bank were under discussion, the Ottawa ' Free Press,' in an article on March 17, in a leading editorial, has the following:
In order to bolster up his case for an investigation into the incorporation of the Farmers' Bank, Mr. Crothers with the idea of showing that ' something was held back ' revamped the story in distorted form of a purely ordinary business transaction which Mr. Calvert had with the said bank.

I shall not read the whole of that article, as it would not edify the members present nor improve the fragrance of ' Hansard.' What I did say on that occasion, as will be found at page 5486 of Uurevised ' Hansard,' was as follows:
We have been told-I do not remember whether in this House or out of it-that the person who was chief whip in the Liberal party in this House at that time introduced Travers to the Finance Minister. It has been established-
I think, perhaps, that word ' established,' was a little too strong. I would not use it if I were speaking now, but I did use it then.
It has been established that, shortly afterwards, that chief whip made a loan from this bank-stated by some to amount to $5,000, but, I believe, stated by himself at $3,000, and that loan was charged up to commissions. Something occurred we had not learned yet.
The difficulty seems to be about the statement that this loan was charged up to commissions. My statement was founded on the report of the police court proceedings, as reported in the Ottawa ' Citizen,' and the Ottawa ' Journal,' of February 18, which report was in concurrent terms and was as follows:
Travers had a personal conference with Hon. Mr. Fielding, being introduced by W. S. Calvert, then Liberal whip. Mr. Fielding asked Travers if he had paid anything to Calvert for the latter's friendly interest, and Travers was able to answer truthfully that he had not. Later Calvert was lent $5,000 without security, which was charged to ' commissions ' on the bank's books. This loan, later, was repaid in full.
The proceedings were reported in the ' Evening Telegram,' of Toronto in these words, this being part of the cross examination of Travers under oath:
' What took place between you and Calvert in the delay in getting the certificate?'
' We took it down to Fielding, and we had 15 or 30 minutes interview with him.'
' Did he assist you ? '
That is, Calvert.
' Yes, he said all he could for us.'
Travers swore lie never paid Mr. Calvert anything at any time.
| Did you loan him any money?'
Not then, but I did some months afterwards.
' How much? '
' About $5,000 or $6,000.
Travers said that all had been paid back but $560, and he had heard this was paid since the failure of the bank.
The statement I made that this $3,000 or $5,000, whichever it was, had been charged up to commissions was based on these reports of the proceedings in the police court in Toronto as evidence coming from Mr. CROTHERS.
Travers under oath, and not made without any foundation whatever as charged in this article.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair I desire to request certain information from the hon. the Minister of Marine (Mr. Brodeur), and with that end in view I will ask permission to read a letter which I have this moment received:
Sorel, March 20, 1911. My Dear Mr. Blondin, M.P.,
This is to inform you that I have been dismissed by the department from St. Joseph de Sorel. It happened on Friday evening when my presence card was taken from me.
I immediately spoke to the chief, Mr. Papineau, who told me that he knew nothing about the matter. I also saw Mr. Badeau, head of my department, who also professed ignorance on the subject. This means that the timekeeper has taken upon himself to dismiss me on the order of Mr. A. Aroham-bault, assistant to Mr. Oscar Champagne, at present in Ottawa.
Ask Champagne why he dismissed me.
Yours truly,

That Mr. Senecal is the witness, Andromi-que Senecal, who came here last week and gave evidence in the investigation now being carried on concerning Marine Department matters at Sorel.
I wish to inquire of the minister whether he gave orders to any one in the department to dismiss that witness, and also if it is his intention to permit attempts at intimidation of witnesses and thus to prevent us from obtaining, in the course of this investigation, independent evidence free from all constraint.

speakerposition: Minister of the Naval Service; Minister of Marine and Fisheries

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member, I may say that I have given no orders for the dismissal of Mr. Senecal. I should add, however, that I understood from the witness himself when he gave his evidence here that he had left the government service.

The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Maddin) yesterday called attention to two returns which he said had not been brought down, one relating to the

appointment of fish wardens in Victoria county, from 1906 to 1910 and another as to the fish bounties paid in the south riding of Cape Breton at the same time. I must inform my hon. friend that on February 28 last I iaid before the House the return concerning the fish bounties. The other report is being prepared by the officers of my department. The hon. member will see that he has asked for the name, length of service and amount paid to each of these wardens. Owing to the demand for the length of service, the return involves more than a few days copying, as it is necessary to look into all the reports and records of each of these guardians. If my hon. friend does not insist on the length of service, I may get the return to-morrow.

I had no notice of the return having been brought down, and on five or six occasions I called at the office of Mr. Polkingliorne and inquired for the Teturn. I must say in justice to Mr. Polk-inghorne that on none of these occasions was he in the office. With regard to the fish wardens, I asked a similar question in the House in 1909 for the year 1908, and the information was furnished concerning about 125 appointees, as an answer to a question, in a very few days. The additional years would only multiply the work by four, and I trust that the minister will let me have that return as promptly as possible as I am quite interested in having it.

speechtext: Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to call attention to an article published in the ' Globe ' newspaper yesterday, which reads:

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATEMENT IN ' GLOBE 5 RE DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT.

speechtext:
Attempt to Delay Passage of the Reciprocity Agreement.
To Concentrate on Supply Vote. Continuation of Present Tactics Might Necessitate Appeal to Country.
(Special Despatch to The Globe.)
Ottawa, March 19.-With the ending of the fiscal year less than two weeks away, and a very small percentage of Supply for the coming year voted, despite the persistent efforts of the government, and with the obvious obstruction of the opposition, particularly during the past two weeks, it has been decided by the government to devote most of the balance of the month to endeavouring to get Supply, leaving the less urgent matter of passing the reciprocity proposals over until next month.
The article goes on to say:
The government will, by attempting to force Supply during the next two weeks, compel the obstructionists to clearly show their hand, and in the event of a continuation of the present tactics and a refusal to pass an interim Supply Bill, if found necessary, it might be that an appeal to the country would be found necessary to solve the deadlock. The issue in that event would be clearly defined, and although it would be obviously unjust for the opposition to force an appeal to the country before another session, when the Redistribution Bill could be put through and the west given its proper representation in new members, the onus would lie with the opposition, and the government would not fear the result.
Further on it says:
It is probable that Supply will be the first order of government business for the next two weeks, with probably one day in each week given to the continuation of the debate on reciprocity. The developments of the two weeks, with the government's determination to keep the House sitting late unless some progress is made, should serve to put the situation clearly before the people of Canada.
I would like to point out that the article says that the less urgent matter of passing
the reciprocity proposals will be left over until next month, and it concludes in these words:
It may be noted that during the past two weeks the business of legislation and the voting of supplies has practically not been advanced a single step. It may also be asserted with assurance that the government has no intention of either dropping or modifying its reciprocity proposals, and will use every en- _ deavour to have them passed by the House as " speedily as possible.
These two statements seem to contradict each other. Now, as every one in the House knows that article is absolutely untrue, and the ' Globe,' with its usual indifference to truth, evidently pays no attention to what transpires in this House.
I have gone through ' Hansard,' and counted up the columns occupied by Liberal members and Conservative members respectively, to see exactly who has been guilty of obstruction, if there has been any obstruction. On the 28th of February, when the discussion on reciprocity was resumed, there were 80 columns taken up by the Liberals and none by the Conservatives. On the 2nd March reciprocity was again up and there were 54 columns taken by the Liberals and 29 by the Conservatives, while on the matter of the health of Ottawa nine columns were taken by the Liberals, making 63 in	all for the
Liberals that day.	On the 23rd of
March the questions before the House were: the garnishment of civil servants' salaries and the Hague Tribunal, and on that day there were 32 columns taken by the Liberals and 44 by the Conservatives. On the 6th of March the subjects under discussion were the Lanctot matter, Ottawa's health, the Hague Tribunal and Supply, and on that day 42 columns were taken by the Liberals and 29 columns by the Conservatives. On March the 7th reciprocity was again before the House, and there were 43 columns taken by the Liberals and 40 by the Conservatives. On March the 8th reciprocity was again before the House, and there were 68 columns taken by the Liberals and 27 by the Conservatives. On March the 9th reciprocity was again discussed, and there were 53 columns taken by the Liberals and 48 by the Conservatives. On March the 10th the Minister of Railways brought in his annual statement, and he and his Liberal friends occupied 67 columns, as 'against 19 columns by the Conservatives. On March the 13th the Georgian Bay canal, was discussed, and there were 39 column® occupied by the Liberals as compared with 19 occupied by the Conservatives. On March the 14th the question of the capitalization of the railways introduced (by the hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean), was before the House and including a speech by the member for North Cape Breton on reciprocity the Lib-

erals occupied 33 columns that day and the Conservatives 47. On March the 15th and 16th the question of the Farmers' Bank was under discussion and the Liberals occupied 73 columns these two days as compared with the Conservatives 142, that being a field day for the Conservatives. On March the 17th several matters were before the House including the question of health, the question of the speech made by the lion, member for North Oxford, alien labour, and the reading of resolutions in regard to reciprocity, after which the House went into Supply. Yesterday, the resolution of the Minister of Railways was before the House and the Liberals occupied 46 columns and the Conservatives 33. A summary of this from and including the last day of February up to date gives 687 columns of ' Hansard ' filled with speeches from the Liberals and 549 columns occupied by Conservative members. If we exclude the discussion on the Farmers' Bank, and every one will admit that the members on this side were justified in bringing that up, then the Liberals have occupied 614 columns to 407 by the Conservatives. During all this time we have only had an opportunity of discussing reciprocity on portions of five days, and while the Conservatives have filled 162 columns of ' Hansard ' on the question of reciprocity the Liberals have filled up 335. In view of these figures it is up to the ' Globe ' newspaper to apologize, although I do nqt expect that it will. This article in the ' Globe ' accuses the opposition of obstruction, and it says that in consequence of that obstruction the government may be forced to go to the country. It looks to me as though the government were paving the way to go to the country as they know that the longer, these proposals are before the people the more obnoxious they become. At all events the figures I have given prove that if the government do decide to go to the country and deprive the west of the extra representation to which it is entitled the onus and fault and blame will rest on the shoulders of the government and not on the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, my attention has been called to a statement made referring to me by the member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie), in his speech on reciprocity on the 14th instant, when I was not present in the House. He said:
I received from a member from the west this afternoon some evidence that seems to me very striking. In the great province of Saskatchewan they have 51 members local and Dominion, and I am told on the authority of an hon.
Mr. MIDDLEBRO
member from that province that out of the 51 there is only one man who is opposing this pact and that man is the hon, member for Qu'Appelle in this House. A11 the rest are in favour of the agreement.
The hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) has been already taken to task by the hon. member for East Hastings (Mr. Northrup), because of a serious misrepresentation of that gentleman's attitude made in the course of the same speech, but his statement regarding me has been quoted outside of this House where the hon. gentleman (Mr. McKenzie) is not so well known as he is inside or I would not take the trouble to call attention to it. He had no warrant whatever for making the statement he did. I have so far refrained from expressing any opinion one way or the other. When I have a statement to make I will make it myself, and will not ask the hon. member for North Cape Breton to make it for me. He is one of the last men in the House to whom I would make that request. This is a matter of immense importance, and while the government supporters had no difficulty in endorsing the proposals the moment they were laid before the House and the country, and the moment they heard the barest outline of them, or even before they heard it at all, I have felt it my duty to carefully weigh every bit of information available before coming to a decision. That information has been meted out to us in a most niggardly way. It has had to be dragged out of the government item by item like drawing teeth. The House has a right to complain of the meagre information supplied, in such marked contrast to that supplied to Congress by the American government to enable them to study the question from every point of view. In some respects we are even now dependent on information supplied by the American government which our government should have supplied. But we want more information still than the American government has supplied, and along lines which it was not necessary for them to give. We want information in regard to the trade and prices in Australia and New Zealand, and the other British colonies and in Argentine and the other favoured nations which are to have free entry to our markets which is denied to us in their markets. I am justified in saying that no one in the House has yet had the information necessary to enable him to make a satisfactory study of the full effect of the agreement. It is only within the last few days that important statements have been made on the subject by the Prime Minister, and the Finance Minister which alter in a material degree the bearing of this whole question; and while it will no doubt still further add to the satisfaction of such manufacturers as

are endorsing these proposals-and there are many of them-it will on the other hand be received with bitter disappointment by those farmers who are also supporting it in the hope of getting a square deal.
On Friday last the attention of the House was called by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Campbell) to a report appearing in the ' Globe1 newspaper of a speech delivered at Woodstock, Ontario, by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt). The hon. member for Dauphin used these words:

Mr. Speaker, there is a matter that I wish to bring to your consideration and to the consideration of this House. 1 do it because I see that the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) is in his seat. It is a matter that has been brought up already in this House by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). It is with regard to an article that appeared in the ' Globe ' of date Saturday, March 4, of this year. At a meeting at Woodstock, in Ontario, the hon. member for North Oxford, in addressing the people there spoke as follows:	The speech is so good I shall read it
all:
' With regard to reciprocity, he noted that very little had been heard about the consumer's interest. He did not believe the reciprocity agreement being negotiated would affect the price to the consumer adversely. That might seem strange, as it was supposed the farmer would get a better price.'
He was addressing, I understand, an aggregation of men who were more or less engaged in manufacturing. He went on to say:
' He could not see that manufacturers would be touched very much, as few articles manufactured in Canada were affected. He was sure the Bain and Woodstock wagon companies would compete in the world's markets even with 21- per cent reduction in the tariff. He thought the manufacturers opposed reciprocity because of what might follow, the ' thin end of the wedge,' but he had been assured

'
This is what I want to bring to your notice: '-he had been assured by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Fielding that nothing of the sort would follow. They had gone as far in the farmers' interests as they would.'
As a farmer and a representative of farmers, I want to emphasize that point that one of the most aggressive members on the Liberal side of the House, one of the strongest supporters of the First Minister and his government, in a public meeting gives his word as a member of this House to the people of Woodstock, a manufacturing centre, that he has the word absolutely of the First Minister and the Minister of Finance that the farmers' interests would not be conserved any further than was dope by. this agreement. He goes on to say:
' It would be foolish for us to think of tinkering with the tariff or putting it on an unstable basis.'
He was talking to manufacturers.
' Therefore, the present government, in his 131
view, would not tinker any more with it unless to make some minor adjustments.'
This matter was brought up by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), and the First Minister in reply said:
' With regard to the other question, I think my hon. friend had better wait until the hon. member for North Oxford is in his seat.'
This is the first opportunity I have had of bringing the matter before the House when the hon. member was in his seat. I hope that he will reply to me either that he is misre-ported in this Liberal newspaper or that he will repudiate this statement. From a farmers' standpoint, I hope he will not say the statement is correct.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can relieve my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) from .answering the question of my hon. friend from Dauphin (Mr. Campbell). I can answer him now. There is no doubt whatever as to the attitude of the government. It has been defined on this floor more than once, the last time it was defined was only two or three days ago, when the Minister of Finance, in answer to a question put to him with regard to the speech of President Taft and that answer will give all the information which my hon. friend wants. The Finance Minister was questioned as to the speech delivered by President Taft at Atlanta, especially to the following extract:
' When we entered upon these negotiations, I asked the Secretary of State and his commissioners to offer free trade in everything, but this Canada could not grant us, because she has a protective system and she was afraid of the competition of our better-organized industries.'
To this the Minister of Finance replied:
' That statement may be entirely correct, and I have no doubt is, as to the instructions that the President gave to his officials. But as to what actually occurred in the conference, the matter did not advance to a position which would enable these gentlemen to make such a formal offer in that way. At the very earliest stage in the negotiations we certainly gave them to understand that we could not undertake to have any free trade in manufactures, speaking generally.
This is the position of the government. We have undertaken to have reciprocity in natural products, not in manufactured products. At the present time our noliov is before the House to have reciprocity in natural products, and I shall li" verv glad if we have the assistance of our friends that far in favour of the farmers. T doubt very much if we will, but we will see what we will do afterwards.
The Prime Minister then continued:
The statement made by the hon. member for North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) was quite consistent with our policy, it was nothing new. and he had perfect authority, not only he but every member of the Liberal side, to make that statement.
Did the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance authorize the member in auestion to make that statement?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have answered that already. It is perfectly true. The bon. member for North Oxford and every Liberal



member had such authority, he was not kept in ignorance of our policy in this matter and knew it well. He only stated what is our general policy.
It may be added that this is in accordance with the answer given to the manufacturers' deputation by the Prime Minister in January last.
During the last few days I have received resolutions from different grain growers' associations in the following terms-they are all alike:
1.	That the reciprocity agreement before the House of Commons be ratified during the present session.
2.	That agricultural implements be placed on the free list during the present session.
3.	That the British preference be increased to fifty per cent of the general tariff at the present session.
If the grain growers had been aware of the government's pledge to the manufacturers, they would not have passed these three resolutions, because the last two are incompatible with the first, and they must accept the alternative between them. If the members of the legislative assembly of Saskatchewan had been aware of the Prime Minister's statement that the present government had gone as far in the farmers' interests as they would, and that they would not tinker any more with the tariff, unless to make some minor adjustments, they also would not have added to their reciprocity resolution the clauses calling for a downward revision of the tariff and an increase of the British preference, because if the reciprocity agreement passes, it precludes a reduction of__the duties on manufactured goods.
In regard to the period for which the government's pledge not to reduce the tariff holds good it must not be forgotten that in the exchange of letters that took place between the American and Canadian representatives it is expressly stated that while either party is free hereafter to make changes it is hoped and expected that the arrangement will remain in operation for a considerable period. The Minister of Finance has stated that the government are in honour bound to make every endeavour to carry out the understanding contained in the correspondence.
At the great farmer's delegation which was heard in this House on the 16th December last the memorial on the Customs tariff was presented by Mr. MoCuaig with the remark that it was the most important of all the requests presented that day.
The arguments used by nearly every speaker on its behalf were levelled at the undue protection granted to the manufacturers and the burden thus imposed upon the farming community. Mr. B. McKenzie, secretary of the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association and editor in chief of the Mr. LAKE.
' Grain Grower's Guide,' in the longest and most exhaustive speech made on the subject touched on no other point and from beginning to end confined himself to a reasoned demand for the reduction of the excessive protection now enjoyed by the manufacturers. Under this agreement it now appears that almost the sole benefit to the farmers is that they are to be allowed 'to sell their products in a free market, but they must continue to buy their implements and all the necessaries, including such natural products as coal, coal oil and lumber, in a highly protected one. It seems impossible to believe that Mr. Mackenzie, who has for weeks been in such close touch with the government and the Liberal members, has been in ignorance of what has now come to light. Yet the * Grain Grower's Guide ' has so far given no intimation of it to the farmers of the northwest.
In the reciprocity negotiations we* were informed that the Canadian commissioners would not even listen to the offer of the Americans for any reciprocity in manufactured goods. The farmers delegation specially asked amongst other things for free trade in agricultural implements, machinery, vehicles, illuminating fuel and lubricating oils, cement and lumber. The only concessions they get in regard to any of these items is a reduction in the duty on agricultural implements and cement, so small as to be of practically no material advantage to them. And the condition attached to the so-called reciprocity in natural products-which by no means includes all natural products-

I have allowed communications, telegrams, &c., concerning reciprocity to be read on the motion to go into supply; but as the House has referred the reciprocity resolutions to the Committee on Ways and Means, I do not think that a specific discussion of the reciprocity question can be in order at this stage.

I have no intention of entering into a specific discussion of the question at all, but I am merely making a statement of facts very much along the line of those made in the House on a resolution to go into supply. I do not intend to argue the question from any point of view but wish simply to make what I understand to be a statement of the facts:
And the condition attached to the so called reciprocity in natural products-which by no means includes all natural products-is that the present government will positively not tinker any more with the tariff for a considerable time to come unless to make some minor adjustments. At this session the government has turned down the proposals of the opposition for government abattoirs and chilled meat system, for the government operation of terminal elevators, and for a sub-

stantial reduction, of tlie duties on agricultural implements.

The hon. gentleman said a moment ago that the government had turned down the proposition of the opposition for a reduction of the duties on agricultural implements. Is that the policy of the opposition which has been turned down by the government?

The hon. gentleman may draw what conclusions he chooses in regard to that matter, the fact still remains that the government turned down a resolution on that subject. I firmly believe that for a time advantages will accrue to the farmers of the northwest from the free entry of their grain and cattle into the United States market. It will give better competition for these products and they will be better assured of getting their true value. It must not be forgotten, however, that both countries have a surplus, and the price of the whole is finally fixed by the value of that surplus in the Liverpool market.
It is true that it has been generally expected that the democratic party now coming into power in the United States would have materially reduced or taken off altogether the duty on food products and raw materials whether this agreement had been entered into or not. But apart from that I have from the first been favourably disposed to the pact both on account of the free entry of our grain into the United States, and also from the belief that it was a step which was certain to be followed by a reduction of the present high protection on manufactured goods.
On the other hand the principle laid down by the government that the measure must be accepted or rejected as a whole now appears in the view of the government's latest statement to involve the acceptance of their now declared policy that there shall be no further substantial reduction of the duty on any manufactured goods. This is a policy I will not accept. It changes the whole situation.
The hon. gentleman must admit that he is now discussing reciprocity, and that cannot be done except in committee.
I have just but a couple of minutes more when I shall conclude.
If the hon. gentleman is allowed to do that, every other member can do the same thing.
I am merely making a personal explanation.

The hon. gentleman must submit to the rule of the House and not discuss anything which has been referred to in the committee except in committee.
181 i
If my hon. friend is violating the rules, there have been at least a dozen others who have been guilty of the same violation.

I have said that on the motion to go into supply, telegrams and resolutions might be read, but no one could enter into a specific discussion of the question of reciprocity which has been referred to the committee. I am in the hands of the House. The older members know what the custom is in a matter of this kind.

I wish merely to say a few words with regard to the statement made by the right hon. the Prime Minister the other day and also to ask for some information from the government with regard to this most important question. The right hon. the Prime Minister states that every Liberal member was aware of the government's policy in this respect and knew it well. I presume they were informed in caucus. They kept it well to themselves, for though I had strong suspicions that it might be so, I had up to Friday last no positive information. Nor, I am sure are the people generally aware of this condition, especially in the northwest.
It therefore appears that Liberal members and the Liberal press have been trying to have this matter rushed through before all its phases and all its significance have been thoroughly before the people.
It cannot become effective before the American Congress has dealt with it, which will not be for some time yet. In the meantime the government should compile further statistics in regard to the prices of the various commodities dealt with both at Canadian and American centres and also at the principle points in the British colonies and the favoured nations which may come into competition with our farmers in the Canadian home markets. Also statistics should be compiled in regard to the exports of those countries to other nations as well as to Canada, and such further information which will give parliament and the country generally a clearer understanding of what they are doing. In the meantime the valuable discussion which has been taking place in the House should be continued from time to time by those who have information to impart. This is too big a question to be decided without the fullest investigation.
May I ask a question?
That is out of order.
Is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lake) opposing the reciprocity agreement because it does not provide for reciprocity in manufactured articles?
I have made a definite statement, and the hon. gentleman can take what comfort he likes from it.

And whereas interprovincial and inter-Im-pcrial trade are on a fairly prosperous and developing foundation' under existing fiscal arrangements ; therefore,

In view of the fact that the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Fowke) read a resolution from certain people in Oshawa, I think it' well to place on ' Hansard ' the exact terms of a resolution passed by a very influential body of men, the Board of Trade of the town of Kentville, in the constituency represented by the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden). I believe that resolu tion was referred to in the House, but the exact terms of it do not appear in ' Hansard.' It is as follows:
Whereas the adoption of the proposed reciprocity agreement between Canada and the United States would substantially reverse the policy which has brought Canada to- her present prosperous and enviable position and cause widespread disturbance in her trade and injury to many interests, and jeopardize the commercial and political status of the Dominion,
And whereas it would hamper Canada's freedom in developing her own resources in her own way and by her own people,
And whereas it would check the growth and development of trade between the various provinces and parts of Canada with each other and between Canada and the empire, and would diminish Canada's position and influence as a unit within the British Empire.
Therefore, resolved that this_ Board places itself on record in protest against the adoption of such reciprocity agreement.
This resolution was passed after a discussion of several hours. The meeting was held after ample notice was given, was largely attended and was presided over by the President of the Board of Trade who happens to be one of the most influential and best known fruit men of the Annapolis valley. I believe that the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Borden) referred to the fact that a resolution had been passed by the Board of Trade of Kings county,
but that resolution was passed prior to the resolution which I have just read, and my information is that it was passed at a small meeting of which ample notice was not given, and there was no discussion. If I am credibly informed, the matter is to be reintroduced for discussion by that board, when we shall know the reai views of its members.

The statement I made the other day as to the action taken by the Kings county board of trade was absolutely correct. The meeting was not a small meeting. The vote was carried in favour of reciprocity by 87 to 2, which would not indicate a small meeting. Also, it was held in daylight and the vote-was taken in daylight. The vote on the resolution to which my hon. friend (Mr. Rhodes) refers was taken between one and two o'clock in the morning, and in the dark -a deed of darkness. The only fruit grower or farmer, or man directly interested in fruit-growing, the principal industry of Kings county, was the president. The meeting was called ostensibly to transact other business, but, in the course of the evening, the secretary of the Tory party of Kings countv
A fruit man.

No, a lawyer, not a fruit-grower and not interested in fruit growing-the secretary of the Tory party brought in the resolution, and it was seconded by my former opponent, Mr. Webster, another lawyer. The discussion was kept up until the electric light service of the town, which is a partial service, had ceased, and no vote was taken. I do not know that it is material whether the resolution was passed in daylight or in darkness, I. cannot see that the question >of light or darkness would affect the hearing of those at the meeting, but my information is that this resolution was passed rmahimously and I have that authoritatively from the secretary.

Any proposals the United States may make for reciprocity with Canada will receive careful consideration from the Dominion government, but the attitude of the Canadian people is to let well enough alone. . . . The predominant note in public affairs in Canada to-day, is contentment with its present lot and hope that the future may bring forth closer relations with the mother country.
I was somewhat amused the other day when the Minister of Militia was listening to the Prime Minister making light of this cry, ' Let well enough alope,' applauding the Prime Minister's utterances. At the time this extract came into my mind. Is that a correct report of the speech delivered at Boston on that occasion?
Of course the minister has already spoken on this resolution. With the consent of the House the minister can speak again.

I feel greatly flattered to observe that the hon. gentleman from York not only reads my Mr. SEXSMITH.
speeches made in Boston, but watches my countenance to see how I accept the views expressed by the Prime Minister of this House.
Denouncing those which you expressed.

No, not at all. Since the question has been put I may say that I had the honour of being invited to address a meeting of Canadians in Boston some time ago, and although I cannot remember exactly the remarks I made, the impression I endeavoured to give was very much on the line of this quotation. I do not think I used the words ' Let well enough alone,' but I had no idea at that moment that the authorities of the United States would accept a treaty with this country on the lines which the ministers who went to Washington were able to secure. I had in view that which I had for the last 15 or 20 years believed to be in the minds of the United States that no treaty would be made with this country which did not include free trade in manufactures, and from that point of view, I thought, and I still think, it would be advisable for us to remain as we are. But, Mr. Speaker, I never was foolish enough and, representing a county such as mine, I would not be wicked enough to refuse to accept from the United States an open market for our agricultural products in that country, the greatest blessing which could possibly be conferred upon the producers of natural products, particularly agricultural products and fruit in this country.
I would call the attention of the House to the following despatch :

Shepherd, member of the Council of the Consolidated Boards of Trade of Saskatchewan, asserted to-day that all the boards of trade in that province were opposed to reciprocity, as were also a majority of other people.

I have been veTy much interested by the play of argument on the question of this reciprocal arrangement, hy the deft reading of resolutions and extracts from papers. It is a thing which in my experience is novel in the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

One would have been astonished 10 or 15 years ago to have an

episode like this take place. What I am asking myself and would like to ask the first Minister and the Speaker is, what kind of a House we are going to have if this irregular mode of procedure is allowed to go on. Mr. Speaker seemed to have had a hazy idea that in going into supply we ought not to be allowed to take up and discuss the question of reciprocity, the reciprocal pact which has been referred to the Committee of Ways and Means. In that I believe he is correct, but the reading of every one of these resolutions and all the discussion we have had for the last half hour, which might go on for 55 hours so far as any objection from the Speaker or the House is concerned, is clearly a violation of the rule which the Speaker laid down. I am not at all censuring or attempting to censure the members who have been engaged in this interesting form of discussion. It has brought out many points. I just end as I began, by asking whether or not we propose to allow the House to drift into this irregular method of proceeding. If so I do not know what will become of us as a deliberative body, and I do not quite see how we shall ever get through with the business.
