I have your letter of July 20th suggesting arbitration. What you propose is what I offered Messrs. Berry & Murdock in my letter of July 8th. It is also wliat I proposed in my letter to you of July 13th, to which in yours of July 15th you replied:	'I regret
that it does not seem to me that I have the requisite authority to take either of the courses you suggest, nor do I believe it would he in the public interests to do so/ While your attitude appears to have changed, I infer from the report statement of the views of Messrs. Murdock & Berry, as contained in the morning papers, that they maintain the same position they have taken from the beginning.
Yours truly,
(Sgd.) CHAS. M. HAYS, President.
Apart from the fact that the department might have thought of referring this matter to arbitration, apart too from the fact that Mr. Nesbitt in his report had suggested it, _ there was this singularity that both parties all along had been in favour of arbitration. The Grand Trunk railway were in favour of	arbitration,
the men were in favour of arbitration, and the principle had been accepted by both. The' only difference between them was as to the tribunal to whom the differences should be referred to. It is not a part of my duty here this afternoon to stand in judgment between the men and the railway company, but the men, on the one hand, contended that the two arbitrators to whom the matter should be referred were two gentlemen on the other side of the line who had acted with regard to similar matters in dispute with a number of American railways, and who had standardized the rates in the States. The men were in favour of arbitration, but insisted that these two arbitrators should be appointed. On the other hand, the Grand Mr. NORTHRUP.
Trunk was equally in favour of arbitration, but insisted that the matter be referred to a board composed of experienced railway men with the obligation of abiding by the result of the finding. If ever there was a case in which the department, which is supposed to act the part of conciliation, which is supposed to prevent strikes and to put an end to them as soon as possible in case they do occur, in which one would think that the wisdom of referring the matter of arbitration would_ occur at once, it was in such a case as this and, in spite of the fact that both parties desired arbitration, and the only difference was as to the composition of the tribunal, a difference which might have been settled by an appeal to the Minister of Labour and which might have been settled by the exercise of the law provided by the government, no suggestion whatever was made of arbitration until after the unhappy strike had commenced.	.	.
Now, in view of these facts is not one justified in saying that no general demand had been made for arbitration? For six months the difference had existed between the company and the men and for months it had been acute. For months the Conciliation Board had been sitting and nearly a month lapsed from the time it gave its report until the strike actually occurred. Yet during all that time not one finger was raised, not one suggestion was made by the Minister of Labour in favour of arbitration even although the president of the Grand' Trunk Railway Company says that he himself suggested this arbitration to the minister on the 13th of July. As soon as the strike had really commenced the suggestion was then made by the Minister of Labour that there should be arbitration. On the 20th of July the minister writes to each of the parties concerned pointing out that it is rendered imperative in the public interest that means be found to affect a settlement of the difficulties and the speedy resumption of work * in all branches of the company's service. The answer, it must be admitted, was not very satisfactory. The men promptly declined the suggestion and the Grand Trunk replied that they had offered this before and that the men had refused. The letter of the 21st July of Mr. Hays which I have read, states that he declines to accept the proposition made by the government. But, nothing was done by the government then. Having written that letter to both parties the government seemed to think all had been done that should be done and until the 27th of July, so far as one can judge from the correspondence, nothing practicable seems to have been done by the government other than the writing of letters. Then, it apparently began to dawn on the minister that something really must be

done, and he wired to Messrs. Murdock and Berry representing the men, again suggesting arbitration, and asking them to consult the head authorities whom they represented to obtain, if possible, their consent to arbitration; the .matter to be referred to some persons who would be mutually acceptable. I think it must be said to the credit of the men that on receiving this appeal from the minister, which was based on grounds of the public interest and in view of the loss which the strike was causing, within 24 hours a reply came by wire which was followed by letter, accepting the proposition of the minister and offering to refer the matter, to the arbitration of some parties mutually acceptable. Mr. Hays, howeveT, took a different position and on page 96 of the report we have this reply as follows:
Montreal, Quebec, July 24, 1910. Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King,
Ottawa. .
Your telegram of the 23rd received, while as you know from the many conferences urging your action before the strike took place and from our offer repeated and urged upon the committee we were desirous of arbitration and so avoiding the existing trouble. The time for such action has now passed and it is only necessary that we should have the protection to which we are entitled to enable us to resume the full operation of the road.

We have now come to the 24th of July, when the first genuine appeal was made by the government to both parties, and the men accepted the offer of arbitration, and the president of the Grand Trunk declined, stating the strike was over and that all the Grand Trunk wanted was sufficient protection for their property to enable them to resume the operation of their road. It must be admitted that if the statement of Mr. Hays were true, it amply justified the position he took. The strike had commenced on the 18th of July and by the 24th of July according to' him, the strike was over, and if that were so, he would be justified, in saying that having beaten the men, all he wanted was protection for his property to resume operation of the road. But, the question arises whether this telegram of Mr. Hays to the Minister of Labour was true or not. No one in the world should better know the truth of the statement than the president of the Grand Trunk, and had the government no evidence to the contrary, they might act upon it, but the first thing it was the duty of the government to do, was to ascertain what was the real truth. It happened that owing to the absence of the Prime Minister, Sir Richard Cartwright, Minister of Trade and Commerce, was acting Prime Minister, and recognizing the gravity of the strike and the injury to Canadian trade, Sii
Richard Cartwright on the 26th of July, two days after Mr. Hays had declared the strike was over, sent a telegram to all the collectors of customs in the province of Ontario asking reports from them as to the manner in which business was being carried on. This is the telegram,:
Ottawa, July, 26, 1910.
Confidential and urgent. Please inform me by wire immediately, not later than noon Wednesday, if possible, extent to which business in your locality is being affected by present strike, to what extent is fright being moved.
Then a letter was sent by Sir Richard Cartwright on the 27th of July to Mr. Hays, after all the answers to this telegram had been received, and that letter reads:
July 27, 1910.
Dear Mr. Hays,-I am inclosing for your information copies of telegrams received this morning by the commissioner of customs in reply to a wire sent last night to the collectors in the several towns and cities of Ontario, asking for information as to the extent to which business is being affected by the present strike. Yon will observe that the replies cover virtually all of the important localities in the province on the Grand Trunk Railway system, and that, without exception, they go to show that up to the present little or no freight has been received or sent out by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, also that in some localities industries are being obliged to close down, while in other localities which are fortunate enough to be served by two roads, the facilities of the other roads are proving inadequate to the demands upon them.
The government has been carefully considering the whole strike situation, and whilst it is the wish of my colleagues and myself to cause yon as little embarrassment as possible, we cannot but feel, in view of the situation as disclosed in these messages, all of which are from an official and strictly impartial source, as well as from many other urgent representations, that it is eminently desirable that some settlement of the present dispute should be immediately effected, and that if this cannot he brought about by a conference between the parties, the matter should be left to arbitration as already suggested by the government.
I very much hope that you may find it possible to co-operate with the government along the lines suggested in its endeavours to deal with the critical situation which has arisen, through the interruption of operations over a large part of your company's system.
Yours very truly,
(Sgd.) R. J. CARTWRIGHT,
Acting Prime Minister.
I shall not read all the answers that came in from the 60 or 70 collectors of customs. The Minister of Trade and Commerce having said in his letter to Mr. Hays that the trade of the country was paralysed, that little or no freight was moving on the Grand Trunk, that many industries had closed down and others would ibe compelled to close down, I shall quote a few sample bricks from the replies sent

to the Department of Trade and Commerce. The first is from Trenton and it Teads:
Trenton, Ont., July 27, 1910. John McDougall,
Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa.
Little inconvenience from strike apparent here to date. Have Canadian Pacific railway and boat connection with Montreal and Toronto, and Merchants' needs supplied in that way. No freight moving on Grand Trunk railway. Loss trifling so far and will not suffer for ten days yet.
ROBERT FRASER, Collector.
That, I think, is about the most favour-ble of all the replies, and that says:
No freight moving on the Grand Trunk.
The next is from Owen Sound:
No Grand Trunk freight trains moving; Grand Trunk not receiving freight! and freight sheds actually closed and business badly affected.
The next is from Orillia:
No freight has been moving since the 18th July. The material cleared here has been merchandise that was on hand. The customs revenue affected by strike would be in the neighbourhood of $1,000.
The next is from Woodstock:
No freight moving on Grand Trunk railway; local business not affected so far.
The next is from Windsor:
Wabash passenger and freight trains leaving Windsor as usual, no interference. Grand Trunk passenger trains leaving Windsor as usual, no delay. Grand Trunk local freight handled by Canadian Pacific and Michigan Central railways. No freight leaving Windsor by Grand Trunk with exception of six car-loads of horses by Canadian express to Fort Erie. Two freight trains from east to Windsor over Grand Trunk since strike was inaugurated.
I will not occupy the time of the House in reading these 60 or 70 communications from the various collectors of customs; but in going through the return brought down by the Minister of Labour, I find, in addition to these telegrams from collectors of customs, that about 100 pages are filled with protests from mayors of various municipalities in the province of Ontario. The first is from Mr. Patterson, mayor of Brockville, dated July 27, urging the government to renew the effort to bring about conciliation; another from Mr. H. A. Currie, mayor of Collingwood, to the same effect; another from a wholesale firm in Hamilton; another from Kincardine, from the mayor; another from Walkerton, from the mayor ; another from Peterborough, from the mayor. There are probably 60 or 70 additional communications!, bearing date the 27th or 28th of July, from mayors of Mr. NORTHRUP.
municipalities and from presidents of boards of trade throughout the country, protesting that business was paralyzed by the strike, and stating that no freight was moving on the Grand Trunk. Therefore the fact is un-c-ontradictable that the government knew cn the 27th and 28th of July, if they could place any reliance on the words of their own collectors of customs and on the words of the mayors of various municipalities, and the presidents of various boards of trade, that the strike was continuing, that practically no freight was being moved on the Grand Trunk, and that trade was being paralyzed throughout the country. Now 1 think I am justified in saying that at such a time as that, when an appeal had ileen made to the government for arbitration, when one side had consented to arbitration and the other side had declined simpjy and solely on the ground that the strike was ver-though the government had in their possession incontrovertible evidence that the strike was not over-the premier and the Minister of Labour might well have used the big stick on the president of the railway to insist on a settlement of this matter by reference to arbitration; and yet nothing of the kind was done.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What is the big stick?

That is an American 'xpression, and as the right hon. gentle man and his colleagues have had more ex perience with the people of that country than I have had, I would hardly venture o instruct him in the American vernacular. The late President of the United States used that expression very frequently.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think my hon. friend used the expression without knowing what it means.

There is no doubt as to the meaning of the expression. The government has a certain power which it can exercise over railway companies and other corporations which are continually asking favours of the government, to compel them to do what is right, and that power is what the late President of the United States described as the big stick. I do not go so far as to say that the government of this country has power to compel railway companies to do what is wrong; but I think their power is irresistible when it is exercised to compel a railway company or any other corporation to do what is right, provided they have public sentiment at their back. The only reason the president of the Grand Trunk gave for declining arbitration was that the iStrike was over; but in face of all these telegrams wdiich came to the government between the 24th of July and the 28th of July from all parts of the province of Ontario, I think the government would have

been amply justified in saying to the president of the Grand Trunk: You have maxle a statement which is not justified by the facts; the only reason you give for refusing arbitration has fallen to the ground, and we insist on arbitration taking place now. Various gentlemen throughout the country who took an interest in this matter aJlso wrote to the government. I find in the .correspondence a letter from Mr. Mills, who is connected with the Mutual Assurance Company of Canada, and one from Mr. Trowern. Secretary of the Retail Merchants' Association of Canada, eminently shrewd, practical business letters, calling the attention of the Minister of Labour to what he might and should do; and I venture to say that the real 'solution of all these difficulties as suggested in these letters. That is not mereilv in an arbitration between the men and the company. If a strike takes place, it is the people of the -country who have to foot the bills. It means an enormous loss to the people who are doing the business of the country. It is the duty of the government to protect these people; and therefore, instead of having simply an arbitrator for the men and another for the company, the only fair wav would be to have an arbitrator for the railway company and another for the men, another for the agricultural interests, another for the mercantile interests, another for manufacturing interests, thus constituting a board sufficiently large and representative to command the confidence of all parties, and then by legislation to have it declared that the finding of that board should be absolute and final. If something of that kind had been done in this instance the country would have been -saved an immense loss which has resulted from this unfortunate strike. But nothing of the kind was done. Not only prior to the strike was nothing done to prevent it, but during the continuance of it nothing practical was done to bring it to an end. At last towards the end of July an appeal came from Messrs. Murdock and Berry stating that they had seen Mr. Hays and nothing could be expected from him, and praying that the Minister of Labour would come to Montreal and see if he could do something. Then for the first time the Minister of Labour took some action. He went to Montreal; and it is a curious fact that Mr. Hays, who on the 24th of July had said that the strike was over, is found three or four days later negotiating for a settlement of the strike. The strike was settled on the 29th or 30th of July.
On the 2nd of August.

The settlement was practically agreed two or three days- before. The Miniser of Labour (Mr. King) did go to_ Montreal and meet the Grand Trunk railway authorities and the men, and an
agreement was come to. I need not weary he House with the terms of this agreement save as to one item, on page 341 of he return, the agreement is set forth, and n it there is this clause:
T-he company will put back as soon as possible the men other than those who have been or may be found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct, the understanding being that there is to be no coercion or intimidation used towards the new men.
The men declined to accept that condition. They said very naturally that if the company was only bound to put the men back as soon as possible, there was no limit to the delay. It might be months or years or never, so that although the men and the company had agreed on the terms, the agreement could not be made operative simply because the men said:	We must
have some definition as to what you mean by putting the men back as soon as possible. Failing to agree, the men left Montreal. The Minister of Labour (Mr. King) and the Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick Bordetn), however, continued their good work, and I give them full credit for what they did at that time; and after two or three days an arrangement was come to, and this wire was sent to Mr. Murdock and Mr. Berry, and also a letter from the minister over his own signature a few days later. The telegram will be found at page 336 of the return. This was the wire sent to James Murdock, representative of the general committee of the Grand Trunk railway and Canadian Pacific railway:
Confidential. Mr. Hays has given Borden and myself an understanding that the men will within three months from this date be taken back into service and within that time be placed in their former positions. All men referred to in agreement signed by both parties. We understand by the men, all men referred to in agreement signed by both parties. In accordance with our understanding with you, I shall expect to hear by wire immediately that the strike has been declared at an end. I will confirm this wire over my own signature.

Minister of Labour.
On that telegram being received by the leader of the men, the strike was, on the 2nd August, called off. Immediately felicitations began to be exchanged between the department and the men over the happy results of the negotiations whereby the men immediately, or within three months at the latest, were to be returned to their former positions. Unfortunately as time went on, the men began to find that these felicitations were rather premature. The men were refused their old places, and put into inferior positions. In fact to such an extent was that done that it seemed almost as if Mr. Hays was in a jocular mood when he

said he would put the men back, for that is what he really did. He put the conductor of a limited on an express train and the ' conductor of an express train on a local. At all events complaints were rife as to the manner in which the Grand Trunk railway was failing to keep its agreement with the men. Unfortunately the department did not seem able to do anything. It seemed to content itself by merely writing a letter now and then protesting to the Grand Trunk railway that the company was not doing what was right by the men, and it suggested that Judge Barron might be appointed to. investigate the complaints. The Grand Trunk railway, however, refused to accept any such proposition, and Mr. Hays wrote this extraordinary letter which will be found on page 468 of the return. The Minister of Labour (Mr. King) had written Mr. Hays urging on him to carry out his agreement, and on the 10th of November this extraordinary refusal was received from Mr. Hays. The House will remember that the agreement was that the men should be put back in their old positions within three months. Mr. Hays writes as follows:
I have yours of November 9. In the opinion of the officers, our undertaking to re-employ all who were not found guilty of acts of violence or disorderly conduct has been complied with.
Here is the extraordinary feature of this letter:
In the interests of good discipline and public safety it is imperative that the officers of the company shall be the sole judge as to the proper qualifications of the employee and his fitness for the duties assigned him. It would, therefore, in our opinion, be prejudicial to the public interests to leave to an outside party, positively unacquainted with the railway service, the determination as to the fitness of any one for our railway service. That responsibility can only be assumed by the proper officials of the company.
So we find this extraordinary state of affairs, that when the president of the Grand Trunk railway had agreed with two ministers of the Crown that he would put the men back within three months and when the men relying on that assurance, had resumed their work, and when the Grand Trunk railway had failed to put the men back, the president of that road, in reply to an appeal from the minister to carry out his agreement, gave as a reason for not doing so that the company had the right to decide as to the fitness of the persons to be reinstated. But the company had been satisfied with these employees. The company had not discharged any of them. The men had gone out voluntarily to the regret of the Grand Trunk railway, and yet after the company had promised two ministers of the Crown that within Mr. NOETHRUP.
three months it would restore these men to their positions, its president dared write to one of the ministers refusing to carry out his pledge and giving as the reason that his company had the right to decide who were and who were not fit for the positions. If ever , there was an opportunity for the ministers to use the big stick, to exert their authority to say to this railway magnate: You cannot break your agreement in- that way, you cannot break faith with these men, who accepted this agreement on the faith of ministers of the Crown-if there ever was an occasion, it was this; and the ministers who would fail to assert their dignity and compel this railway president to carry out the promise he had made to them can hardly expect to command the confidence of this House.
After that letter had been sent on November 10, the Minister of Labour acknowledged it. One would have thought that there would have been an outburst from the Minister of Labour, one would have thought that after the Minister of Labour had received this letter stating such a wilful, deliberate breach of faith, which put the ministers of the Crown in the position of having given a pledge to the men that was not being carried out, the minister would have sent to Mr. Hays such a letter as he would not easily forget. What did the minister say:
Ottawa, Ont., Nov. 12, 1910.
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge and thank yop for your communication of the 10th inst. in reply to mine of the 7th, in regard to employees in train and yard service of the Grand Trunk Railway Company who have not as yet been taken into the company's service.
Yours faithfully,
(Sgd.) W. L. MACKENZIE KING. Chas. M. Hays, Esq.,

Co.,
Montreal, Que.
Now, am I not justified in saying that no genuine, sincere, honest effort was made by the government to secure the return to their places of these men, when, in the face of such a breach of faith as I have just pointed out on the part of the president of the Grand Trunk railway, the minister, instead of teaching him a lesson he would remember to his dying day, wrote thanking him for his communication? A minister who appreciated his position would have notified the authorities of the railway that, if their president was a man who would deliberately make an agreement with a minister on which the minister intended to act and did act, and on which some 3,000 men had acted on the statement of the minister, and afterwards would trv to put a lie in the mouth of the minister, then, for all time to come, he would decline to do business with a man who had so failed to appreciate his

position, and the position, dignity and honour of a minister of the Crown.
Now, the question arose afterwards as to what position was really occupied by the minister at the time this agreement was made. I have read the telegram sent by the Minister of Labour to the men stating that an agreement had been made by Mr. Hays with him and Sir Frederick Borden. Now, let me read you another letter. This is found at page 549 of the Return brought down. It is dated November 29, 1910, and was written by the Minister of Labour to Mr. Murdock. I will not go into the whole letter, but will read only a few extracts:
I have, of course, nothing to say as to the method taken by Mr. Hays. That is his own business. I feel, however, as stated at the interview with Mr Berry and yourself that it is eminently desirable that whatever course may he suggested by Mr. Hays should be followed by men who are seeking reinstatement, provided the course suggested is both feasible and honourable.
And further:
From communications which have been received, it would appear that an effort is being made in certain quarters to hold the government responsible for the non-reinstatement of all of the men involved in the recent dispute. This, as I am sure you will admit, is most unfair, inasmuch as the undertaking as to the reinstatement was given not by the government but by the company, Sir Frederick Borden and myself being in the position of witnesses to such undertaking.
Now. does the minister really appreciate the importance of that statement? First, a telegram is sent, followed by a letter over his own signature, to the men, that an undertaking had been given to them, the ministers. That undertaking is not carried out, and the men are protesting against it not being carried out. Members who sit behind the Minister of Labour are protesting on behalf of their constituents and pointing out that the men by hundreds are being discriminated against and a gross injustice done. When these protests come in, the minister writes Mr. Murdock stating that the agreement was made not by the government, but that 'Sir Frederick Borden and myself ' were ' witnesses to the undertaking.' Could there be a flatter contradiction of what the hon. gentleman himself had wired the men? Witnesses! How could they be witnesses? There must be two parties to an agreement. The men were not there; they had gone away, refusing point blank to be parties to the agreement unless the term ' as soon as possible ' were defined. Then the minister intervened, and an agreement was made, as truly said by wire in the first instance, between Mr. Hays on one side and Sir Frederick Borden and the Minister of Labour on the other, that so and so should be done. And afterwards the minister writes that he is a witness.' Tt is perfectly obvious why
he wishes to be regarded only as a witness. If the agreement were admitted to be made with the ministers, as the minister stated in his telegram and in his letter, then the ministers were responsible for the carrying out of the agreement, because they were parties to it-the men could not be, for they were not there. The ministers and the railway company were the only people there, and therefore, as stated in the telegram, the agreement was made between the railway company and the ministers. And this meant . that it was the duty of the ministers to see that the agreement was carried out. _
I wish to make my remarks as brief as possible, so I will not go over the almost endless correspondence between the parties representing the men and the individual men, with regard to the hardship, the injustice done them by the Grand Trunk authorities in refusing to reinstate them. Tc put the matter briefly and taking the case that was least injurious to and most favourable to the men, a man was put in this position:	If the Grand Trunk authorities decided not to re-employ him, he was compelled to' bring his evidence and go before the very official under whom he had worked and prove that he was innocent. It was the first time in the history of British jurisprudence when a man was asked to prove his innocence, instead of being held innocent until proven guilty. And this proof he had to bring before the official who had dismissed him, and dismissed him, as appears in many cases, without rhyme or reason. To prove himself innocent meant thereby to prove that the official who had dismissed him was wrong. Talk about appealing from Philip drunk to Philip sober! Here wag a case of appealing from Philip sober to Philip sober, and attempting to prove that he had been wrong in the judgment he had given. And if, after trying to prove his innocence, the judgment of this unusual court was against him, he was at liberty to appeal along up the line, and if he succeeded in reaching Mr. Hays, Mr. Hays would be willing to hear him. Is it any wonder that dissatisfaction arose among the men? At last, so much dissatisfaction arose that the government suggested that Judge Barron be appointed, and offered to pay his expenses if he were appointed. But after the president of the Grand Trunk refused to have any person appointed, on the ground that the railway company had the right to decide who were the persons to have in their employ, suddenly, the Grand Trunk did employ Judge Barron. Now, 1 have nothing but the most profound respect for Judge Barron personally. I doubt if any man could be found more likely to act rightly and judiciously in this matter than he. And I am delighted to see that the
Would the hon. member read the first part of that letter?

Certainly. It reads:
Dear Sir,-In further reference to conference held yesterday between the Premier, the honourable Minister of Railways and yourself with a committee of unreinstated Grand Trunk employees accompanied by the undersigned, at which meeting the facts in connection with the Grand Trunk Company's failure to equitably apply terms of settlement made when strike was called off were discussed.
The committee desire to assure you and through you the government that they deprecate the attitude taken by certain gentlemen (presumably well intentioned), whereby an effort is being made to hold the government responsible for the failure to apply the terms of settlement made.
We appreciate fully the assistance given both at the time of the strike, and since, by the government in its efforts to bring about on behalf of the Canadian public and the citizens of Canada, who were involved in the strike, a settlement, and an equitable carrying out of the terms of that settlement. It is definitely understood by the men interested and the undersigned that it is not on account of any failure on the part of the government that.the present unfortunate situation obtains, but that the existing conditions are rather the result of the obstinate disregard for contract obligations on the part of Grand Trunk officials.
The assistance given so far in a conciliatorv ' and mediating way by representatives of the government is much appreciated, but flip committee would further request that if consistent the government should take further means, if possible, either bv the appointment of a Royal Commisison or in some other consistent manner to enforce from the officials of the Grand Trunk an acceptable carryinsr out of the agreement made and understandings reached.
In the subsequent part of that letter they protest against the men who have repudiated the agreement made with the Grand Trunk employees and the understanding reached with ministers of the Crown. As I pointed out one can hardly relieve the ministers of the Crown from the responsibility that rested on them of seeing that the agreement made with themselves was carried out. The men seem to have acted with wonderful forbearance. They seem to be most grateful for any slight crumbs of service that fell to them from the Crown and certainly if ever there was a body of men, if one may judge from the correspondence as set forth by the Minister of Labour, who deserved to have him stand by them, it was the striking employees cf

the Grand Trunk Tailway in the late strike, and I think there is nothing more touching than the fidelity with which up to the last they stood by the minister and the reckless disregard of their interests by the minister whenever the mighty head of the Grand Trunk railway appeared on the scene.
Then there is an interesting correspondence between the men and Judge Barron. There is first a letter from the President of the Brotherhood of Bailway Trainmen, and the vice-president of the conductors to Judge Barron dated January 5, from Toronto. They send a number of names to the judge, of men that they claim have been left off. They also send a number of names of men who were formerly conductors and who were reduced in position saying:
Men who were formerly conductors have been started into service as brakemcn and numbers of men have been continuously employed on inferior trains or in less preferable positions than those occupied prior to the strike.
They also promised to send him a further list. Judge Barron acknowledges that letter on January 10, and says this:
I have now carefully compared your list with that sent me from Montreal. Your list contains 127 names of men, not given me by the Grand Trunk railway to investigate. I have no explanation for this great difference. But I would suggest for your consideration the propriety of every man who wishes to do so (and who has not yet done so) applying for a hearing under section 12, page 10, of the regulations governing employees, and then appealing to the general officers of the company, should the result of the hearing be unsatisfactory. The wisdom of doing this is that if delay arises in the decision for fifteen days, he thereafter receives his regular pay, and furthermore such action brings him within the sphere of my investigation should the railway not reinstate.
In so far as I can see from all the documents and correspondence brought down, that is the only insight we have into the jurisdiction of Judge Barron. We know hd is appointed by the Grand Trunk, we know he is paid by the Grand Trunk, we know he received a list from the men and a list from the Grand Trunk, and that the list from the Grand Trunk contained 127 less names than the list supplied him by the men. Writing on the 10th January he points out the wisdom of a man appealing to the officer who discharged him, and then by regular gradations up to the head of the railway, this action alone bringing the man within the sphere of Judge Barron's investigation. Surely the minister must be willing to impose a little more on these men than he would like others to impose on him if he thinks that the gratitude which they ex-oressed again and again in the early days of this case should be continued to the end when at the most all they get is a tribunal Mr. NORTHRUP.
such as that, and when Judge Barron, in his own letter addressed to Mr. Murdock, the men's representative, pointed out that the only case in which he had the jurisdiction of a sort of Supreme court was when the men had exhausted all courts of appeal from the first man to whom he appealed, the man who had discharged him, up to Mr. Hays and when, if justice had not been done by Mr. Hays, he could appeal to him.

When the House Tose at six o'clock, the hon. member for Hastings (Mr. Northrup) had moved an amendment to the motion to go into Supply to the effect that the House expresses its Tegret in three particulars: first, that the government, through the Department of Labour or in any other way, had wholly failed to make any intelligent effort to avert the late strike; second, that the government had failed to put an end to this strike during

its continuance; and third, that it had failed to compel Mr. Hays, the president of the Grand Trunk railway, to effectively carry out the agreement made with the government. There aTe therefore in that amendment three distinct charges. First, that the government is responsible for not having effectively prevented the strike which took place on the Grand Trunk railway ; second, that the government was responsible for its continuance or failure to terminate it; and third that the government is responsible for the alleged failure on the part of Mr. Hays to carry out the terms of the agreement.
I shall endeavour to deal with these charges in their order; but before doing so it -may enable the House better to understand and appreciate the -significance of the strike and the difficulty of dealing with it if I briefly outline its nature and true proportions. Let me point out first of all that this strike was but the culmination of a movement which started on this continent nearly two or three years ago, on the part of the organizations connected with the railways of the continent to bring about a standardization in the rates oi pay and the conditions under which the men are obliged to labour. I say on the continent, because these brotherhoods have organizations not only in Canada and the United States but also in Mexico. They extend throughout the whole of North America. About three years ago they endeavoured to bring all the railways on the continent on to one plane as respects the conditions under which the workingmen are obliged to labour. That movement, which started in the western states, took up the greater part of the year 1909 in that section of the country. Then having succeeded in bringing about an equalization of conditions on the American roads, they endeavoured to bring a similar condition in western Canada and succeeded, so far as the Canadian Pacific railway was concerned. In 1910, these organizations endeavoured to bring into line the railways in the eastern states. Some 40 or 50, or perhaps 60 different railways were affected; and when these brotherhoods were able to bring about an equalization, making allowance to a certain extent for the differ-ent^ conditions under which men were obliged to work-when they succeeded in bringing into line the whole of the United States and western Canada, they next turned their attention to- eastern Canada. In that connection there were two different railways to be considered-the Grand Trunk railway and the Canadian Pacific railway.
If hon. .members have grasped the significance of what I have said, they will see that the dispute, which finally took the 1821
shape of a strike on the Grand Trunk railway, was -but the culminating point of that movement which had been -successful in every part of North America except in the Dominion as respects the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway. When that point is grasped, hon. gentlemen will perhaps hesitate before endeavouring to hold the government or any one responsible for the fact that that strike came on as it did with the force and effectiveness that characterized it. As I have said, there were only two railways left, after the railways in the eastern states had been brought into line. These were the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway. Under our law before any action can be taken in the nature of a strike, the parties are bound to submit their differences to a board. They applied for boards in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway, and these were granted in each case. The boards met simultaneously and reported in the case of each company. In neither case was the report wholly acceptable to the men, but I believe in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway, that company was prepared to accept the award of the Board of Conciliation, though the men were not. What followed? After the board had given its award in the case of the Canadian Pacific railway the men in the employ of that company expressed dissatisfaction at certain things, and then the Canadian Pacific railway company and the men -came together and negotiated further and armed at a settlement satisfactory to each. -That left the movement then confined en-irely to the Grand Trunk railway. The men had been successful on all the railways in the United States and western Canada and in eastern Canada, with the exception of the Grand Trunk railway, with which they had been unable to bring about a satisfactory settlement. One reason alone is sufficient to account for that fact, and that is that different methods of payment in connection with the two roads the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway, had been in existence. In the case ot the Canadian Pacific railway the men were paid by the mile, and in the case of the Grand Trunk railway by the day. On practically all the railways in the United States, these organizations had been able to -bring about a system of payment by the mile, and the object of the struggle in connection with the recent strike was to compel the Grand Trunk railway to change its system from a day to a mileage basis. The importance of that difference will be apparent when one -considers what takes place as the roadbed and the rolling stock are improved. Where the payment is on the mileage basis, the better the condi-

tion of the roadbed and the rolling stock, the greater the run can be made, and the longer the run, the more the amount of *wages. On the other hand, when payment is by the day, every improvement to the roadbed and the rolling stock calls from the men the expenditure of a greater amount of energy; they have to. travel over a greater distance for the same pay And as the Canadian Pacific railway and the Grand Trunk railway have been improving their roadbeds and rolling stock, the result is that the men on the Canadian Pacific railway were getting a higher rate of wage relatively than those on the Grand Trunk railway. In some cases the difference was as high as 38 or 40 per cent in favour of the men on the Canadian Pacific railway as compared with men doing the same work on the Grand Trunk railway. It was this large difference in the rate of wages and this difference in the method of payment that caused dissatisfaction among the men on the Grand Trunk railway, and it was because this difference was so great that the Grand Trunk railway was not prepared to accede to the demand made on them at the outset nor the terms proposed later on.
My hon. friend in his motion charges the government with not having made any intelligent effort to avert the strike on the Grand Trunk railway; and in endeavouring to impress this on the House, he said there were two ways open to the government by which they could have averted that strike. One was to appoint a board under the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, and the other was to appoint a board of arbitration under the provisions of the Conciliation and Labour Act and compel the two parties to execute the award of that board and thus prevent the possibilities of a strike.
My hon. friend is a lawyer, and I am somewhat surprised that he should have made that criticism because he must be familiar with the laws which this House has enacted; and if he reads through the statutes he will be unable to find any law which gives the Minister of Labour power to compel an arbitration. This parliament has never seen its way to concede compulsory arbitration. And. in the absence of a statute of that kind, I am unable to see how the hon. gentleman could draw the inference he has attempted to draw that the minister had power to compel arbitration.
With the permission of the minister, I desire to ask a question. Is there any question about the jurisdiction of this parliament to pass a compulsory Act? I ask purely for information.

I do not think myself there is any question about it. I think that if this parliament decided that it was a wise Mr. KING.
thing to enact such a law, it would have full power to do so. When the matter was considered some years ago, a Compulsory Arbitration Bill was introduced by Sir Wm. Mulock, then Minister of Labour. That Bill was read twice, I think, in this House, and then copies of it were distributed throughout the country to labour unions and important companies with a request for their opinions as to a law of that kind; and they were pretty nearly unanimous in stating that they did not wish compulsory arbitration, but what they wished was compulsory investigation.
Would there not be an interference with the right of contract if such a law were passed?

So far as railways chartered by this parliament are concerned, I think certainly this parliament would have authority to enact a compulsory arbitration law. However, that is aside from the question. The point I wish to make clear is that there was not the alternative which my hon. friend has suggested.
